‘Bachelor Party D’eux’ movie review: Amal Neerad makes a sequel almost as forgettable as the original
 While parts of the film in the initial half comes off way better than its predecessor, the latter half feels aimlessly written. Overused slow motion both amplifies and drags on some sequence.
 Updated - November 19, 2026 07:32 pm IST 
 S.R. Praveen READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 A still from the movie Bachelor Party D’eux. 
 The thought of making a sequel for a film usually crosses the minds of the makers when the first one is a successful outing and there are interesting elements left to explore. The fact that Bachelor Party (2012) was almost a dud, except for some passable sequences, makes the decision to make Bachelor Party D’eux a perplexing one. Not to forget, it was also heavily inspired from Johnnie To’s 2006 film Exiled .
 Amal Neerad might have been prompted to take this on after seeing the surprising afterlife that the first part had. Over the past few years, Bachelor Party has been talked up as some kind of classic movie in online forums, giving it a status much above than is suggested by its box office numbers. Probably due to this, Amal has left the basic structure of the film untouched.
 Bachelor Party D’eux (Malayalam)
 Direction: Amal Neerad Starring: Naslen, Kunchacko Boban, Nadia Moidu, Tovino Thomas, Soubin Shahir, Sharafudheen, Sreenath Bhasi, Shine Tom Chacko, Chandu Salimkumar, Rajisha Vijayan, Jyothirmayi, Hansika Krishna, Paris Laxmi Plot: Members of a gang, who split due to differences, come face to face with each other when they take up a job. Runtime: 132 minutes So in the second part, we have another gang in Kochi, not learning any lessons from all the missteps that Ayyappan and gang did way back in 2012. But parts of the film in the initial half comes off way better than its predecessor, be it in the organic banter between the lead characters, who first meet in an orphanage, or their evolving equation with a woman who wants to take revenge against the ones who murdered his son’s family.
 Since there are no surprises in store for a film of this nature, a lot depends on how effectively the characters are written. On that count, Amal Neerad who has written the screenplay also (with dialogues by Unni R.) has not managed to do justice to most characters, who don’t stand out for their individuality. Even Naslen, who made such an impact as a chilling antagonist in the recent Tamil film Scene, can infuse only so much life into such a character. Soubin Shahir, who was a misfit as a gangster in Bheeshma Parvam , fits better into a similar role here.
 Amal appeared to be more concerned about recreating some of the sequences from the first part as it is, a surprising wish considering the fate of the first film. So, we have everything from the ethical conflicts within the gang, a drunken confrontation at a dinner table (with the same song reused), a similar cameo (Tovino instead of Prithviraj) and even a post-credit song sequence set in hell (just that the song is better this time around.)
 The overuse of slow motion, for which Amal has been celebrated and lampooned in equal measure, makes some of the sequences seem endless, even as it is effective at some places. The action is nothing to write home about, with the latter half of the film appearing to be quite aimlessly written.
 Bachelor Party never deserved a sequel. Amal Neerad appears to have gone ahead and made one to prove that point.
